narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the second decile is well below the average of sixth decile among accepted students, and this low ranking strongly pushed the model toward expecting you to fail the bar. Your family income was the next most important factor. Being in the middle-income bracket also nudged the prediction toward failure, though less dramatically. Your LSAT score of 35 worked in the opposite direction. Because it sits only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it helped pull the prediction back toward passing, but not enough to overcome the earlier signals.

In short, the model saw your relatively weak first-year performance as the dominant reason you might struggle with the bar, with your family income adding some additional concern.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your grades in the remaining years so your later decile rankings rise, and consider retaking the LSAT to push that score higher. Stronger numbers in either area would likely change the model’s outlook and improve your chances on a future application.
